379.title: Richer isn't better
379.hook: "I'm richer than you, so I'm better" doesn't follow (Enchiridion 44)
379.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes catch comparisons that jump from 'they have more' to 'they are better' and correct the logic, as in Enchiridion 44.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two handles, and the one that can be carried. Your line was he's my brother. Which conflict did you pick up differently? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

A twenty-year class reunion. Name tags, a slideshow, and a low hum of measuring. Who has the bigger house. Who has the better job title. Who still looks thirty. Nobody says the next step out loud, but it hangs in the room: so they're doing better than me. So I'm less than them. Epictetus heard the same hum in his own day, and in section forty-four he does something unexpected with it. He doesn't preach. He checks the logic. Today: richer isn't better.
screen: `A TWENTY-YEAR REUNION.` → `BIGGER HOUSE, BETTER TITLE.` → `RICHER ISN'T BETTER.`

segments.voice: First, two arguments that fail. I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you. I'm more eloquent than you, so I'm better than you. These don't follow, Epictetus says. The conclusion doesn't come out of the premise. Second, two arguments that work. I'm richer than you, so my property is greater than yours. I'm more eloquent than you, so my speech is better than yours. Those are fine. They compare like with like: money with money, speaking with speaking. Third, the hinge, and it's one short sentence. But you, he says, are neither property nor speech. That's the whole move. The comparison is real, but it's a comparison of things you have, or things you do. The jump from my things are bigger to I am better quietly assumes that you are your things. A Stoic says you're not. You're the one who uses them, who judges, who chooses. Fourth, why this is freeing in both directions. It takes the air out of the reunion bragging, of course. But it also takes the sting out of losing the comparison. Their house is bigger. Fine: their house is bigger. That says something true about two houses, and nothing at all about two people. You can admire someone's skill, or envy their savings, and still notice that it doesn't follow. And the same check works on the voice that says I'm worse at this, so I'm worth less. It doesn't follow either.
screen: `RICHER, SO BETTER? DOESN'T FOLLOW.` · `RICHER, SO MORE PROPERTY? FINE.` · `YOU ARE NEITHER PROPERTY NOR SPEECH.` · `IT FREES THE WINNER AND THE LOSER.` · then, large: `DOESN'T FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one comparison that's been running in your head lately. Someone's salary, someone's body, someone's family, someone's follower count. Say the full sentence to yourself, including the hidden last step: they have more, so they're better than me. Now break it the way Epictetus does. They have more. True. So their things are more. True. So they are better? Doesn't follow. Rest there for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Richer isn't better. Epictetus checks the logic: more money means more property, not a better person. You are neither property nor speech. Today's word.
Your line: doesn't follow. Catch one bad comparison today, about someone else or yourself, and say it plainly: doesn't follow. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

myth: Epictetus says being rich is bad
he says richer means more property, which is fine. it just doesn't make you better.
section forty-four is built as a logic check
two arguments that fail, two that work, and the reason why.

fork.setup: at the reunion, an old classmate says: I make twice what you do, so I've done better than you. what does Epictetus say?
options: agree, and feel smaller.
doesn't follow. twice the salary, yes; a better person, no.
find something you're better at, and say so.
fork.reveal: twice the money means twice the money. you are neither property nor speech, so the step to 'better' doesn't follow.

trapdoor: what you thought: money doesn't buy happiness.
what it means: comparing possessions or skills is fine, but jumping from 'more' to 'better person' is bad logic.
what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 44 is a lesson in Stoic logic: the conclusion must be about the same thing as the premise.

380.title: Quickly, not badly
380.hook: don't say someone bathes badly, say quickly, until you know his reasons (Enchiridion 45)
380.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism describe other people's actions in plain, observable terms before making any judgment about them, as Epictetus suggests in Enchiridion 45.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the reunion, and the step from more to better. Your line was doesn't follow. Which comparison did you catch? Day three hundred eighty.

A man walks into the public baths, washes, and is out the door in ten minutes, while everyone else lingers over the hot water, the oil and the gossip. Everyone notices. And everyone has the same word ready: he bathes badly. Sloppy. Rude. Doesn't know how it's done. Section forty-five of the handbook takes that one word and swaps it for another. It's a tiny edit, and it changes what you're claiming to know. Today: quickly, not badly.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE LINGERS AT THE BATHS.` → `ONE MAN IS OUT IN TEN MINUTES.` → `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: First, the swap. Someone bathes quickly, Epictetus says. Don't say he bathes badly. Say he bathes quickly. Someone drinks a lot of wine. Don't say he drinks badly. Say he drinks a lot. Second, the reason. Until you know the judgment behind what he's doing, how do you know it's bad? Maybe the quick bather has a sick child at home. Maybe he's late for work, or the water is cold, or he simply doesn't like crowds. You saw the speed. You didn't see the reason. Third, what you gain. If you keep to this, Epictetus says, you won't end up grasping some impressions clearly and then agreeing to others you never actually saw. In plain words: say only what you saw. Quickly is something you saw. Badly is something you added. The habit protects you from a thousand small, confident mistakes about other people. Fourth, a modern echo. A twentieth-century psychologist, Marshall Rosenberg, built a whole approach to hard conversations, which he called Nonviolent Communication, on a similar first step: separate what you observe from how you evaluate it. You came home at midnight is an observation. You're irresponsible is a judgment. Two very different teachers, a long way apart, each with their own reasons, both noticing that people can hear a description without bracing for a fight. A judgment usually starts one. And we met yesterday's cousin of this idea: richer doesn't mean better. Today's version is shorter still. Quickly doesn't mean badly.
screen: `NOT 'BADLY.' 'QUICKLY.'` · `YOU DIDN'T SEE THE REASON.` · `SAY ONLY WHAT YOU SAW.` · `OBSERVE FIRST, EVALUATE LATER.` · then, large: `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose habits bother you. The coworker who's always late. The neighbor who mows at seven. The relative who checks their phone at dinner. Notice the word you usually reach for: rude, lazy, thoughtless. Now try Epictetus' swap. Late. Early. Often on the phone. Just the description. Say it inside, and notice what happens to the irritation when the judgment drops out. The bell holds the time.
Quickly. Epictetus' swap: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed, but not the reason. Today's word.
Your line: say what you saw. Once today, describe instead of judging, and leave out what you added. Day three hundred eighty.

Epictetus' second example is someone who drinks a lot of wine
don't say he drinks badly. say he drinks a lot.

options: you're a slob.
the dishes were in the sink overnight.

fork.reveal: describe what you saw. until you know the reason behind it, you don't know it's bad.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be judgmental.
what it means: describe what you actually saw, quickly, a lot, late, and leave out the verdict you can't see.

381.title: Show the wool
381.hook: sheep don't show the shepherd their fodder, they show wool (Enchiridion 46)
381.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism avoid calling themselves Stoics or explaining philosophy uninvited, and try to let it show in how they act instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quick bather, and the verdict you can't see. Your line was say what you saw. What did you describe instead of judging? Day three hundred eighty-one.

Somewhere tonight, someone who just finished a book on mindfulness is explaining it at dinner, while visibly not being mindful. Maybe we've been that someone. You've been on this path a long time now, nearly four hundred days. It would be natural to want to talk about it. Section forty-six of the handbook has a word for that urge, and then it gives us a strange picture: a field of sheep. Today: show the wool.
screen: `EXPLAINING MINDFULNESS AT DINNER.` → `NEARLY FOUR HUNDRED DAYS IN.` → `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and don't talk much about your principles among people who haven't asked. Do what follows from them. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat. Eat as one ought. Second, Socrates. Epictetus says Socrates had so completely given up showing off that people would come to him asking to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them. He let himself be overlooked, and didn't mind. Third, the test. When someone tells you that you know nothing, Epictetus says, and it doesn't sting, then you can know you've begun the work. And if talk among people new to all this turns to principles, mostly keep quiet. There's a danger, he says, of throwing up what you haven't digested yet. That's not a polite image. He means it not to be. Fourth, the sheep. Sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest the pasture inside, and what comes out is wool and milk. So, he says, don't show people your principles. Show them the actions that come from digesting them. The point lands softly. Talk is the grass. Practice is the wool. People can't use your grass. They can use your wool: a moment of patience, a gossip skipped, a promise kept without swearing. After nearly four hundred days, a good sign of this path may be something someone else notices in you, without you ever mentioning where it came from.
screen: `DON'T CALL YOURSELF A PHILOSOPHER.` · `SOCRATES LET HIMSELF BE OVERLOOKED.` · `DON'T THROW UP UNDIGESTED GRASS.` · `SHEEP SHOW WOOL AND MILK.` · then, large: `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think back over this path: the words, the stories, the practices. Is there one thing that has actually changed in how you live? Not something you could explain, something you do. A pause before reacting. A smaller portion. A kinder answer. Find it. That's your wool. Now picture using it today, without a word about where it came from. The bell holds the time.
Pasture. What a sheep digests quietly inside, giving back wool and milk, not the grass itself; show practice, not principles. Today's word.
Your line: practice is the wool. Show practice today, not talk: let one thing you've learned show up in what you do, and say nothing about it. Day three hundred eighty-one.

the actions that come from them

options: give a short talk on Stoic self-control.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be a know-it-all.
what it means: don't display your principles; digest them, and let what comes out be action people can use.
what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 46 joins Socrates, who let himself be overlooked, to the sheep who give wool, not grass.

382.title: In secret
382.hook: if you live simply or drink only water, don't announce it (Enchiridion 47)
382.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep their personal disciplines private, so the practice serves their own growth rather than other people's admiration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sheep, who give wool, not grass. Your line was practice is the wool. What did you do today that showed it, without a word? Day three hundred eighty-two.

Day four of a new habit. No sugar, or a cold shower every morning, or a run at six. And there it is, the itch to mention it. A casual line at lunch: oh, I don't eat sugar anymore. A photo of the sunrise from mile two. Half the pleasure of a discipline, for a lot of us, is people knowing we have it. Epictetus saw this itch in his students, and in section forty-seven he names it, with a picture of a famous philosopher hugging a frozen statue. Today: in secret.
screen: `DAY FOUR OF A NEW HABIT.` → `THE ITCH TO MENTION IT.` → `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Once you've trained your body to live simply, Epictetus says, don't preen about it. If you drink only water, don't announce at every chance: I drink water. Second, the statue. If you want to train yourself for hardship, he says, do it for yourself, not for those outside. Don't go hugging statues. That's a jab at an old story. Diogenes the Cynic, the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says, used to embrace statues covered in snow in winter, to toughen himself. Epictetus admired Diogenes deeply, but he knew how easily a hard practice becomes a public performance. Third, the cold water. When you're very thirsty, he says, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. A small, private test that nobody sees. That last part, tell no one, is the whole practice. Fourth, why secrecy matters. A discipline you announce starts working for the audience. You get the reward early, in other people's admiration, and the habit quietly changes its purpose. A discipline you keep secret has only one job: to change you. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about giving to the poor in the King James words: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Two teachers, two different reasons, each in its own house, and a shared picture: some good things grow best in the dark, like roots. Yesterday was about showing the wool. Today is about the part of the work that nobody ever needs to see.
screen: `DON'T SAY: I DRINK WATER.` · `DIOGENES AND THE SNOWY STATUES.` · `SPIT OUT THE WATER. TELL NO ONE.` · `ANNOUNCED, IT WORKS FOR THE AUDIENCE.` · then, large: `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one discipline you keep, or would like to: a walk, a fast, a kindness, a limit on your phone, a habit of prayer or quiet. Ask yourself honestly: who knows about it, and do I want them to? Now choose one small discipline to keep entirely secret today. Picture doing it, and picture not mentioning it, even when there's an opening. The bell holds the time.
In secret. Enchiridion forty-seven: train for yourself, not for those outside. Spit out the cold water, and tell no one. Today's word.
Your line: tell no one. Keep one discipline today, do it, and don't mention it, not even once. Day three hundred eighty-two.

pairs: spit it out, tell no one

he says train for yourself, not for those outside.
the snowy statue story is told about Diogenes the Cynic
the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says he embraced snow-covered statues to toughen himself.
Epictetus says to announce a discipline so friends keep you accountable
his practice ends with tell no one.

what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 47 jabs at Diogenes' snowy statues, a Cynic practice that could turn into performance.

383.title: Signs of progress
383.hook: the one making progress blames no one, praises no one, and claims to know nothing (Enchiridion 48)
383.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review Epictetus' signs of progress, especially blaming no one, as a quiet self-check at the end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cold water, spat out, and told to no one. Your line was tell no one. Did you keep one discipline quiet all day? Day three hundred eighty-three.

How would you know if any of this is working? Progress bars are easy when it's a language or a marathon. Words learned, miles run. But a calmer mind doesn't come with a counter. Epictetus' students wanted to know the same thing: am I actually getting anywhere? Section forty-eight answers them with a checklist. It isn't the checklist anyone expects. There's nothing on it about feeling peaceful, or knowing more. It's mostly about what you stop doing. Today: signs of progress.
screen: `HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?` → `A CALM MIND HAS NO COUNTER.` → `SIGNS OF PROGRESS.`

segments.voice: First, two positions. The ordinary person, Epictetus says, expects help or harm to come from outside. The person on this path expects help or harm to come from inside, from their own judgments. Second, the checklist. The one making progress blames no one. Praises no one. Finds fault with no one. Accuses no one. Says nothing about themselves as if they were somebody, or knew something. When they're blocked, they look to themselves. When they're praised, they laugh quietly to themselves at the one praising. When they're criticized, they don't defend themselves. Third, the patient. Such a person, he says, goes about like someone recovering from an illness, careful not to disturb something that's healing before it has set firm. That's a gentle picture. Progress here isn't a trophy. It's a mending bone, and you walk carefully on it. Fourth, the word. The Stoics called this prokopē, progress, and the one making it a prokoptōn. Notice that Epictetus doesn't describe arriving. He describes someone on the road. That's why the checklist matters. You'll never be told you've arrived. But you can notice, on an ordinary Tuesday, that you didn't blame anyone for the traffic, didn't need the compliment, didn't defend yourself against the remark. Those are the signs. Small, quiet, and real. Notice which sign leads the list. Not courage, not wisdom. Blame no one.
screen: `HELP AND HARM COME FROM INSIDE.` · `BLAMES NO ONE, PRAISES NO ONE.` · `LIKE SOMEONE RECOVERING, CAREFUL.` · `PROKOPĒ: SOMEWHERE ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BLAME NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Run Epictetus' checklist slowly, as a mirror, not a test. Blames no one. Praises no one, finds fault with no one. Says nothing about being somebody. Laughs a little at praise. Doesn't defend against criticism. Which one is closest to true for you lately? Which is farthest? Pick one sign to watch for in yourself today, and hold it gently, like a bone that's still mending. The bell holds the time.
Prokopē. The Stoic word for progress, and the one making it. Its first sign, in Enchiridion forty-eight: blame no one. Today's word.
Your line: blame no one. Check one sign in yourself today. When something goes wrong, notice the urge to blame, and let it pass. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: Live the book
384.hook: proud of explaining Chrysippus? better to live what he wrote, and keep your principles like laws (Enchiridion 49–50)
384.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism choose a single principle from their reading and try to act on it for a day, rather than reading or explaining more.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prokopē, progress, and the checklist that starts with what you stop doing. Your line was blame no one. When did you feel the urge to blame, and let it pass? Day three hundred eighty-four.

There's a kind of person you meet at the gym. They know everything about protein timing, muscle fibers, the right angle for every lift. They'll explain it to you at length. They rarely lift. Philosophy has the same person, and so do plenty of hobbies: the one who can explain the book better than anyone, and whose life looks nothing like it. In Epictetus' school, the books students were proud to explain were by Chrysippus. Section forty-nine takes aim at the explainers. Today: live the book.
screen: `THE GYM EXPERT WHO NEVER LIFTS.` → `THE BOOK EVERYONE EXPLAINED.` → `LIVE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school, and the ancient biographers say he wrote more than seven hundred works. And Epictetus' own joke implies he was hard to read. So in Epictetus' day, a student who could explain Chrysippus felt rather proud. Second, the deflation. When someone boasts that he can explain Chrysippus, Epictetus says, tell yourself: if Chrysippus had written clearly, this man would have nothing to boast about. Then he walks through it. What do I want? To understand nature and follow it. I find out Chrysippus explains it. I can't follow him, so I find someone who can explain Chrysippus. So far, nothing to be proud of. Explaining is only the doorway. Third, the turn. When I've found the explainer, what's left is to put the teaching into practice. That alone, Epictetus says, is something to be proud of. If all I admire is the explaining, I'm a grammarian, not a philosopher, just explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer. And when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I blush, because I can't show actions that match the words. Fourth, the next section turns it into a rule. Whatever principles you've taken on, keep them like laws, as if breaking them would be a kind of sacrilege. And whatever people say about you, pay no attention. That isn't yours. Here, it's a fair question. Not how much can I explain. Which one line am I actually living?
screen: `CHRYSIPPUS: BRILLIANT, AND HARD.` · `EXPLAINING IS ONLY THE DOORWAY.` · `I BLUSH WHEN MY ACTIONS DON'T MATCH.` · `KEEP YOUR PRINCIPLES LIKE LAWS.` · then, large: `LIVE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think back over everything you've read or heard on this path, or in any book that mattered to you. Let one line rise up, the one that's stuck. Maybe it's two handles. Maybe it's wait. Maybe it's something older. Say it to yourself once. Now picture one moment today where you could live it, not explain it. See yourself doing it, in plain clothes, in an ordinary room. The bell holds the time.
Chrysippus. The Stoic writer whose books were hard to explain; explaining him is only the doorway, what counts is actions that match the words. Today's word.
Your line: actions that match the words. Live one line you've read today. Pick it, do it once, and don't explain it to anyone. Day three hundred eighty-four.

screen: `DAY 384 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

385.title: How long will you wait?
385.hook: you're not a child anymore, and Socrates became himself by attending to reason in everything (Enchiridion 51)
385.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism return to Enchiridion 51 when they notice themselves postponing something important, and take one small step that same day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chrysippus, the explainers, and the one line you actually live. Your line was actions that match the words. Which line did you live? Day three hundred eighty-five.

Monday. That's when it starts. Or the first of the month. Or after the holidays, after this project, after the kids are older, after things calm down. There's a thing you're going to begin, maybe, and a date it's going to begin on, and the date keeps moving. Near the very end of the handbook, Epictetus stops giving rules and turns to his student with a question. It's aimed straight at that moving date. Today: how long will you wait?
screen: `MONDAY. THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.` → `THE DATE KEEPS MOVING.` → `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: First, the question. How long will you put off thinking yourself worthy of the best things, Epictetus asks, and never crossing what reason tells you? You've received the principles you ought to accept. You've accepted them. So what teacher are you still waiting for, before you start setting yourself right? Second, the plain fact. You're not a boy any longer, he says. You're a grown adult. If you keep being careless and lazy, adding delay to delay, setting one day and then another for when you'll start paying attention to yourself, you'll fail to notice you're not making progress, and you'll live and die an ordinary person. Third, the games. Whenever something hard or pleasant, or glorious or shameful, comes along, he says, remember: the contest is now. The Olympic games are here. They can't be put off. Progress is saved or lost by a single defeat, a single giving way. The Greek word for contest is agōn, the word for the games. Fourth, Socrates. This is how Socrates became who he was, Epictetus says: by paying attention to nothing but reason in everything he met. And you, even if you're not yet Socrates, should live as someone who wants to be. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: doesn't follow. Quickly, not badly. Show the wool. In secret. Blame no one. Live the book. Each of them could start today.
screen: `WHAT TEACHER ARE YOU WAITING FOR?` · `NOT A BOY ANY LONGER.` · `THE CONTEST IS NOW.` · `LIVE AS ONE WHO WANTS TO BE SOCRATES.` · then, large: `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Name the thing you've been meaning to start. The call, the practice, the apology, the application, the first page. Notice the date you've been giving it: Monday, next month, someday. Now ask Epictetus' question, kindly but honestly: how long will you wait? Then find the smallest first step that could happen today, small enough that there's no reason to postpone it. Picture taking it. The bell holds the time.
Agōn. The Greek word for a contest, the games that can't be put off; you're grown, and the contest is now. Today's word.
Your line: the contest is now. Start the thing today, even if it's only the smallest first step. Day three hundred eighty-five.

original.note: Greek: a contest or struggle. In Enchiridion 51, the contest is now.

trapdoor: what you thought: stop procrastinating.
what it means: you're grown and already have the principles; the contest is today, and no teacher is coming to start it for you.
what a scholar hears: agōn, the Olympic contest; Epictetus holds up Socrates, who attended to nothing but reason, as the model.
